12 weeks to a longer ruck

For regular ruckers working toward a comfortable 20–30 km walk or a first longer event.

12 weeks · 4 training days · distance · Updated 2026-11-24

Who this is for

Start only if you already complete a 90-minute familiar-load ruck comfortably and recover by the next day. The weekend times are examples; distance depends on your pace, terrain and stops.

A normal training week

Tuesday: 35–50 minutes easy. Thursday: 25–35 minutes strength (2–3 sets of 6–10 squats, hinges, step-ups, rows and carries). Friday or Wednesday: 20–35 minutes easy cycling or walking. Weekend: the outing below. Avoid hard leg training just before it.

Week by week

  1. 1: 90 min; record pace, stops and comfort.
  2. 2: 105 min; keep weight and terrain familiar.
  3. 3: 120 min; practise food and water.
  4. 4: 75–90 min; easier week.
  5. 5: 135 min; choose a route with exit points.
  6. 6: 150 min; use planned refill stops.
  7. 7: 165 min; keep the same load.
  8. 8: 105 min; easier week.
  9. 9: 180 min; rehearse event kit only if already familiar.
  10. 10: 195 min; practise pacing the second half.
  11. 11: 120–150 min; reduce workload and check recovery.
  12. 12: Target outing at a sustainable effort; if needed choose a shorter finish, not a forced distance.

How to adjust

If your planned event requires substantially more time than your longest comfortable outing, extend this programme with repeatable training blocks rather than making one large jump. A finish target is optional; neither 20 nor 30 km is guaranteed.

Further reading

  • Petersen, A. (2026, January 5). How PATHFINDER training works. PATHFINDER Ruck Training. — Public overview of an independent commercial training approach; these plans are original and are not its paid materials.
  • Orr, R., Pope, R., Lopes, T. J. A., Leyk, D., Blacker, S., Sanz Bustillo-Aguirre, B., & Knapik, J. J. (2021). Soldier load carriage, injuries, rehabilitation and physical conditioning: An international approach. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 18(8), 4010. — Background reading on load carriage, strength, aerobic work and progression; military workloads are not civilian prescriptions.
